units.title: Social Studies Inquiry Practices and Processes

topics.title: Wisconsin students will construct meaningful questions that initiate an inquiry

subtopics.title: Develop questions based on a topic

outcomes.text: Explain why or how a teacher or text provided question is important to a topic or issue.
When provided with a question, determine what other questions are needed to support the research (i.e., "What more do we need to know?").

topics.title: Wisconsin students will gather and evaluate sources

subtopics.title: Gather diverse sources (electronic, digital, print, and other mass media) applicable to the inquiry

outcomes.text: Brainstorm what resources would be valuable to guide the inquiry.
Review and ask questions about books, photos, artifacts, websites, and other sources that will give insight into the inquiry.

topics.title: Wisconsin students will develop claims using evidence to support reasoning

subtopics.title: Develop claims to answer inquiry question

outcomes.text: With prompting and support, state a claim to answer a question that the class is considering.

subtopics.title: Cite evidence from multiple sources to support claim

outcomes.text: Determine which evidence in teacher-provided sources support a claim that answers a compelling question.
Explain how evidence supports a claim for a class inquiry.

topics.title: Wisconsin students will communicate and critique conclusions

outcomes.text: Communicate conclusions.
Respond effectively to questions about their inquiry.

topics.title: Wisconsin students will be civically engaged

outcomes.text: Explore opportunities for personal or collaborative civic engagement with community, school, state, tribal, national, and/or global implications.

units.title: Behavioral Sciences

topics.title: Wisconsin students will examine individual cognition, perception, behavior, and identity (Psychology)

outcomes.text: Understand we are individuals influenced by our relationships and environments.
Identify situations and places that impact a person's emotions. .

topics.title: Wisconsin students will investigate and interpret interactions between individuals and groups (Sociology)

outcomes.text: Describe how groups of people are alike and different.
Understand ways people change and adapt to new situations in places and within a family.

topics.title: Wisconsin students will assess the role that human behavior and cultures play in the development of social endeavors (Anthropology)

outcomes.text: Compare a belief in one culture to one in a different culture (e.g., How do people in a different country celebrate their birthday?).

topics.title: Wisconsin students will examine the progression of specific forms of technology and their influence within various societies

outcomes.text: Describe specific types of technology and demonstrate how they are used on a daily basis for social or cultural purposes.

units.title: Economics

topics.title: Wisconsin students use economic reasoning to understand issues

outcomes.text: Differentiate between a "want" and a "need".
Describe resources that are important or useful to you, your family, community, and country.
Predict a person's change in behavior in response to different potential rewards.

topics.title: Wisconsin students will analyze how decisions are made and interactions occur among individuals, households, and firms/businesses (Microeconomics)

outcomes.text: Differentiate between buyers (consumers) and sellers (producers).
Define product market and categorize prices of products in a local market.

subtopics.title: Firm/Business Behavior and Costs of Production

outcomes.text: Predict how producers use the factors of production (i.e., land, labor, human and physical capital, and entrepreneurship) to make goods, deliver services, and earn profits.

topics.title: Wisconsin students will analyze how an economy functions as a whole (Macroeconomics)

outcomes.text: Identify the cost of everyday goods (e.g., milk, bread, fruit, vegetables, cheese).
Categorize types of money (e.g., coins, bills), and explain why money is used.
Formulate reasons why people save.

topics.title: Wisconsin students will evaluate government decisions and their impact on individuals, businesses, markets, and resources (Role of Government)

subtopics.title: Economic Systems and Allocation of Resources

outcomes.text: Hypothesize how a good gets to the local community market.
Classify different jobs people have and how these jobs help others.
Explain what major public, private, and tribal institutions (e.g., schools, police, fire station) do for people.
Summarize goods and services that the government provides (e.g., roads, schools, police), and how they help people.
Give an example of an unintended cost or benefit to an event (e.g., getting new playground equipment, receiving a present).
Investigate how people can benefit themselves and others by developing special skills and strengths.
Hypothesize why people in one country trade goods with people in another country.

units.title: Geography

topics.title: Wisconsin students will use geographic tools and ways of thinking to analyze the world

outcomes.text: Recognize the difference between maps (paper or digital) and globes, and why someone might choose one over the other for a given task.
Identify physical and human characteristics of a place using maps, graphs, photographs, and other representations.
Construct a map (paper or digital) of a familiar place (i.e., bedroom, classroom, playground) using title, compass rose, and symbols.

topics.title: Wisconsin students will analyze human movement and population patterns

outcomes.text: Analyze where and why people live in certain places.
Classify the local community as rural, suburban, urban, or tribal.
Explain why people have moved to and away from their community.
Describe population changes in their community over time.
Identify and explain differences between rural and urban areas.

topics.title: Wisconsin students will examine the impacts of global interconnections and relationships

outcomes.text: Analyze how different access to resources can create stress in a society (e.g., Who sits closer to the bathroom? Who gets to the lunchroom first?)
Compare and contrast the different modes of transportation and communication used by families in work and daily lives.

topics.title: Wisconsin students will evaluate the relationship between identity and place

outcomes.text: Categorize characteristics of the local community (e.g., weather/climate, population, landforms, vegetation, culture, industry).
Describe how certain places have meanings that distinguish them from other places. (e.g., shopping mall, park, places of worship).

topics.title: Wisconsin students will evaluate the relationship between humans and the environment

outcomes.text: Provide examples of human changes to the environment surrounding the school or neighborhood.
Identify natural resources (e.g., fertile soil, forests, mining) of a place and provide examples of how those resources are used.

units.title: History

topics.title: Wisconsin students will use historical evidence for determining cause and effect

outcomes.text: Identify one or more causes of an event, issue, or problem.
Identify one or more effects of an event, issue, or problem.

topics.title: Wisconsin students will analyze, recognize, and evaluate patterns of continuity and change over time and contextualization of historical events

subtopics.title: Patterns stay the same over a period of time

outcomes.text: Identify patterns of what stayed the same to self, family, and community over time.

subtopics.title: Patterns change over a period of time

outcomes.text: Identify patterns of change to self, family, and community over time.
Explain how something happening outside of your home can affect your family.

topics.title: Wisconsin students will connect past events, people, and ideas to the present; use different perspectives to draw conclusions; and suggest current implications

outcomes.text: Describe a person or event from the past that reflects your own life in some way.
Explain why two people can talk about an event from different viewpoints.
Explain how something from the past can affect your life now.

topics.title: Wisconsin students will evaluate a variety of primary and secondary sources to interpret the historical context, intended audience, purpose, and/or author's point of view (Historical Methodology)

outcomes.text: Describe the events that led to the creation of a primary source.
Identify the intended audience for whom the primary or secondary source was created.
Create one primary source about your life.

subtopics.title: Wisconsin students will evaluate a variety of primary and secondary sources to interpret the historical context, intended audience, purpose, and/or author's point of view (Historical Methodology)

outcomes.text: Point of View (POV)
Identify the POV of your own primary or secondary source.

units.title: Political Science

topics.title: Wisconsin students will identify and analyze democratic principles and ideals

subtopics.title: Values & Principles of American Constitutional Democracy

outcomes.text: Describe symbols, songs, and traditions that identify our state and country.
Assess the importance of rules and laws at home, in school, and in the community.

subtopics.title: Origins & Foundation of the Government of the United States

outcomes.text: Compare contributions of two or more influential people related to the founding of the United States.

topics.title: Wisconsin students will examine and interpret rights, privileges, and responsibilities in society

outcomes.text: Compare rights and responsibilities within the classroom, school, and community.
Classify basic rights that all humans have (i.e., life, liberty, safety).
Summarize situations where individuals have rights, freedoms, and equality.
Develop an opinion about an issue in your school or community.

subtopics.title: Asserting and Reaffirming of Human Rights

outcomes.text: Identify groups within school, community, or society and compare their rights and responsibilities (e.g., student/teacher).
Investigate ways in which people and groups can influence decision makers in school, their communities, states, or country (i.e., voting, running for office, participating in meetings).

topics.title: Wisconsin students will analyze and evaluate the powers and processes of political and civic institutions

outcomes.text: Describe and explain the effect an action has on members of a group.
Express an opinion and vote on a topic in their lives.
Identify different types of media and sources.
Explain why we have elections.
Summarize basic roles of civic institutions (e.g., school, home, family, community).

Compare basic political institutions (e.g., what a government is and how it differs at the city, state, tribal, country, and global level), and the roles they serve in their lives and in the lives of others (e.g., make laws, create order).
Predict how people come up with different ideas to solve a problem.

topics.title: Wisconsin students will develop and employ skills for civic literacy

outcomes.text: Compare and contrast perspectives on the same topic.
Give an example of a compromise.

units.title: Behavioral Sciences

outcomes.text: Describe how a person's understanding, perceptions, and behaviors are affected by relationships and environments.
Describe how culture, ethnicity, race, age, religion, gender, and social class can help form self-image and identity.

topics.title: Wisconsin students will investigate and interpret interactions between individuals and groups (Sociology)

outcomes.text: Compare how people from different cultures solve common problems, such as distribution of food, shelter, and social interactions.
Give examples of how peoples from different cultures develop different values and ways of interpreting experiences.

topics.title: Wisconsin students will assess the role that human behavior and cultures play in the development of social endeavors (Anthropology)

outcomes.text: Investigate how interpretations of similarities and differences between and among cultures may lead to understandings or misunderstandings.

topics.title: Wisconsin students will examine the progression of specific forms of technology and their influence within various societies

units.title: Economics

topics.title: Wisconsin students use economic reasoning to understand issues

outcomes.text: Use economic reasoning to compare and contrast the costs and benefits of a decision.
Categorize different limited resources (e.g., money, materials, time, labor/workers, land, natural resources, renewable or non-renewable).
Infer potential incentives in a real-world situation.

topics.title: Wisconsin students will analyze how decisions are made and interactions occur among individuals, households, and firms/businesses (Microeconomics)

outcomes.text: Compare two product markets found in the local community.
Differentiate between goods and services.
Assess the roles of consumers (demand), producers (supply), prices, non-price factors (e.g., drought or a fad item), and competition in the product market.

subtopics.title: Firm/Business Behavior and Costs of Production

outcomes.text: Compare the skills and knowledge required to produce certain goods and services.
Provide an example of the factors of production (i.e., land, labor, capital, entrepreneurship) for a given product.

topics.title: Wisconsin students will analyze how an economy functions as a whole (Macroeconomics)

outcomes.text: Investigate how the cost of things changes over time.
Describe the role of money, banking, and savings in everyday life, including why people borrow money and the role of interest.

topics.title: Wisconsin students will evaluate government decisions and their impact on individuals, businesses, markets, and resources (Role of Government)

subtopics.title: Economic Systems and Allocation of Resources

outcomes.text: Trace the chain of supply for a needed product (e.g., food, shelter).
Assess the role of economic institutions (e.g., banks, government) in helping individuals and society.
Differentiate between private property (e.g., factories and homes) and public property (e.g., parks, public schools, and government buildings).
Discuss reasons a government taxes people.
Predict unintended costs and benefits (i.e., externalities) for a given current situation or event.
Compare and contrast specialization in two or more regions (e.g., Midwest and Northeastern United States; United States and Japan; Europe and South America).

units.title: Geography

topics.title: Wisconsin students will use geographic tools and ways of thinking to analyze the world

outcomes.text: Summarize how location (absolute and relative) affects people, places, and environment.
Construct maps (paper or digital), charts, and graphs using appropriate elements (i.e., date, orientation, grid, scale, title, author, index, legend, situation)
Identify purposes of and differences among maps, globes, aerial photographs, charts, and satellite images.

Create and label a map (paper or digital) of the local community, state, tribal lands, and country, including both physical (e.g., oceans and continents) and human (e.g., roads, buildings) characteristics.
Identify and construct regions (digital or paper) in Wisconsin and the United States.

topics.title: Wisconsin students will analyze human movement and population patterns

outcomes.text: Categorize the populations of people living in their state and country.
Compare and contrast types of communities (i.e., rural, suburban, urban, or tribal), and different types of places on Earth (e.g., community, state, region, country/nation).
Investigate push and pull factors of movement in their community, state, country, and world.
Describe population changes in their state, and country over time.
Summarize positive and negative factors of cities.
Identify the location and patterns of cities within our state and country.

topics.title: Wisconsin students will examine the impacts of global interconnections and relationships

outcomes.text: Classify a provided set of resources as renewable or nonrenewable, and analyze the implications of both at the local, national, and global level.
Classify various ways that people and countries depend on one another.
Summarize how transportation and communication have changed economic activities over time.

topics.title: Wisconsin students will evaluate the relationship between identity and place

outcomes.text: Describe how certain places may have meanings that distinguish them from other places (e.g., cemetery, places of worship, state/national parks, historical park/battlefield).
Compare and contrast the human characteristics of rural, suburban, urban, and tribal locations in Wisconsin and the United States.
Identify and describe how people may view places in the community differently (e.g., students and senior citizens responding to a new playground).

topics.title: Wisconsin students will evaluate the relationship between humans and the environment

outcomes.text: Compare the positive and negative effects of human actions on our physical environment (e.g., availability of water, fertility of soils) over time
Examine how human actions modify the physical environment when using natural resources (renewable and nonrenewable).

outcomes.text: Use evidence to draw conclusions about probable causes of historical events, issues, and problems.
Use evidence to draw conclusions about probable effects of historical events, issues, and problems.
